rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Aḥmad, Muslim, al-Nasāʾī and others report from Abū Hurayra that Abū Jahl threatened the praying Prophet, recoiled at a trench of fire, terror and wings, and heard that angels would seize him; the sūra was then revealed from 96:6 to its end.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة أن أبا جهل حلف باللات والعزى لئن رأى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يصلي

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the commentators agree that the servant being stopped from prayer is the Messenger and the forbidding man is Abū Jahl.
rows.anchor: كما قال ابن عطية في أن العبد المصلي هو رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم والناهي هو اللعين أبو جهل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies the forbidding man as Umayya b. Khalaf, who stopped Salmān from praying; al-Ālūsī says this is hardly sound because Salmān embraced Islam in Medina while the sūra is Meccan.
rows.anchor: وقول الحسن هو أمية بن خلف كان ينهى سلمان عن الصلاة لا يكاد يصح لأنه لا خلاف

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān relates that the prayer in question was the noon prayer.
rows.anchor: حكى أبو حيان صلاة الظهر

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: A further account calls it the first congregational prayer in Islam: the Prophet prayed with Abū Bakr and ʿAlī; Abū Ṭālib passed with Jaʿfar, urged him to join his cousin, and left pleased.
rows.anchor: وحكي أيضاً أنها كانت تصلي جماعة وهي أول جماعة أقيمت في الإسلام وأنه كان معه عليه الصلاة والسلام أبو بكر وعلي

rows.speaker: أبو طالب
rows.claim: The cited poem attributed to Abū Ṭālib calls ʿAlī and Jaʿfar trusted kin in hardship and urges them not to abandon the Prophet but to support their maternal and paternal cousin.
rows.anchor: وأنشأ يقول : إن علياً وجعفراً ثقتي *** عند ملم الزمال والكرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī questions the Abū Ṭālib account: prayer was prescribed on the Night Journey, usually dated a year before the Hijra, whereas Abū Ṭālib died about three years before it. Reports place the Journey five years after the mission, a chronology criticized by others.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا نظر لأن الصلاة فرضت ليلة الإسراء بلا خلاف وادعى ابن حزم الإجماع على أنه كان قبل الهجرة بسنة

rows.speaker: ابن حزم
rows.claim: Ibn Ḥazm claims consensus that the Night Journey was one year before the Hijra; Ibn Fāris gives one year and three months, and al-Suddī one year and five months.
rows.anchor: وادعى ابن حزم الإجماع على أنه كان قبل الهجرة بسنة وجزم ابن فارس بأنه كان قبلها بسنة وثلاثة أشهر وقال السدي

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ reports al-Zuhrī's view that the Night Journey occurred five years after the prophetic mission; al-Nawawī and al-Qurṭubī favor it, though al-Ālūsī notes objections to that dating.
rows.anchor: حكى القاضي عياض عن الزهري ورجحه النووي والقرطبي أن الإسراء كان بعد البعث بخمس سنين لكن قيل عليه ما قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says nahy means forbidding; its wording suggests Abū Jahl could do no more than that, though some reports indicate he also verbally forbade the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والنهي قيل بمعنى المنع وعبر به إشارة إلى عدم اقتدار اللعين على غير ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Abū Jahl verbally told the Prophet, as he prayed, that he had forbidden him to do so; al-Tirmidhī authenticated this report.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج أحمد والترمذي وصححه وغيرهما عن ابن عباس قال «كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يصلي فجاء أبو جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future-oriented wording evokes the past scene vividly because it is unusual, drawing the audience into the confrontation.
rows.anchor: والتعبير بما يفيد الاستقبال لاستحضار الصورة الماضية لنوع غرابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arāʾayta means ‘tell me’: because seeing leads to knowledge, asking whether one saw functions as asking about what is seen; this usage can apply to visual or mental seeing, though grammarians differ.
rows.anchor: والمراد من أرأيت أخبرني فإن الرؤية لما كانت سبباً للعلم أجري الاستفهام عنها مجرى الاستخبار عن متعلقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one syntactic analysis, the first object of the first arāʾayta is the relative clause; the corresponding objects in the next two are elided, while their second object is ألم يعلم. The earlier conditional answers are omitted and inferred from that answer.
rows.anchor: والمفعول الأول للأول الموصول وللثاني والثالث محذوف وهو ضمير يعود عليه أو اسم إشارة يشار به إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted objects are explained as semantic ellipsis rather than تنازع, since whole clauses cannot be elided in that construction; the text compares this to successive أخبرني clauses and says ألم يعلم signals the conditional answers.
rows.anchor: وليس ذلك من التنازع لأن الجمل لا يصح إضمارها وإنما هو من الطلب المعنوي والحذف في غير التنازع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī reads a three-stage rebuke: first the ban on prayer is condemned without regard to the forbidd er's claimed or actual state; then it is condemned even if he claims guidance or urges piety; finally it is condemned given his actual denial and turning away, with divine sight and punishment underscoring each stage.
rows.anchor: والحاصل أنه تعالى شنع وأوعد على النهي عن الصلاة بدون تعرض لحال الناهي الزعمي أو الحقيقي ثم شنع وأوعد جل وعلا عليه مع التعرض لحاله الزعمي

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority do not restrict the conditions to al-Ālūsī's layered stages: being guided while forbidding worship or urging piety while commanding idolatry is impossible, so the conditional wording feigns concession and mocks the forbidding man; the next condition restates the point as his certain denial and turning away.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على عدم تقييد ما في حيز الشرطيتين بما ذكرنا حيث قالوا إن كان على طريقة سديدة فيما ينهى عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes the first arāʾayta as visual and the next two as mental; the relative is the first object's antecedent, the last object is ألم يعلم, and the middle object is supplied from it. The last clause is uncoordinated to mark its actual occurrence and ensuing threat.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن الرؤية في الجملة الأولى بصرية فلا تحتاج إلى مفعول ثان وفي الثانية والثالثة قلبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis makes all three arāʾayta mental: the first takes the first conditional and its omitted answer as its second object, the second repeats the first, and the third independently contrasts with it; ألم يعلم answers the second condition while the first answer is omitted.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن أرأيت في الجمل الثلاث من الرؤية القلبية والمفعول الأول للأولى الموصول ومفعولها الثاني الجملة الشرطية الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view treats the second and third arāʾayta as repetitions of the first; both conditions fill its second-object position, ألم يعلم answers the second, and the first answer is omitted because the later one makes it understood.
rows.anchor: وقيل أرأيت في الجملتين الثانية والثالثة تكرار للأولى والشرطيتان بجوابهما سادتان مسد المفعول الثاني

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: A grammatical objection says the conditional clause cannot itself be the second object of arāʾayta, which Abū Ḥayyān and others require to be interrogative (or, as in al-Irshād, oath-like).
rows.anchor: واعترض أيضاً جعل الجملة الشرطية في موضع المفعول الثاني لا رأيت بأن مفعولها الثاني لا يكون إلا جملة استفهامية كمانص عليه أبو حيان وجماعة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān objects that a conditional answer expressed as an interrogative requires fa; he says no one permits omitting it except in necessity or poetry. Al-Damāmīnī likewise finds the proposed parsing of هل يهلك in 6:47 problematic without fa.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان إن وقوع جملة الاستفهام جواباً للشرط بغير فاء لا أعلم أحد أجازه بل نصوا على وجوب الفاء

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafājī answers that the conditional and interrogative clauses can together occupy the object and answer positions, either directly or by implication; al-Raḍī and al-Damāmīnī say this accords with Sībawayh's preferred analysis.
rows.anchor: وقال الخفاجي إن جعل الشرطية في موقع المفعول والجملة الاستفهامية في موقع جواب الشرط إما على ظاهره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is taken by some to include anyone capable of understanding and by others to address humankind, as in إلى ربك (96:8); these analyses exclude both the forbidding man and the one forbidden from the direct address. Al-Baḥr prefers the Prophet as addressee, while others allow the disbeliever.
rows.anchor: واستظهر في «البحر » جعله للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وجوز غيره جعله للكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tanwīn on servant is read as indefiniteness; another view says it magnifies the Prophet, the enormity of forbidding him, and the audience's astonishment.
rows.anchor: والتنوين في عبداً لتفخيمه عليه الصلاة والسلام واستعظام النهي وتأكيد التعجيب منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent antecedent of the hidden pronouns in كان and the following verbs is the man who forbids prayer.
rows.anchor: والضمائر المستترة في { كان } وما بعد من الأفعال للناهي

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ instead assigns the pronouns in كان and أمر to the praying servant, and those in كذب وتولى and يعلم to the forbidding man: the servant is guided and urges piety, while his opponent denies and turns away.
rows.anchor: وقيل الضميران في أن كان وأمر للعبد المصلي والضمائر في كذب وتولى ويعلم للذي ينهى وحاصل المعنى على ما قال الفراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take أو as an alternative marker of division; another takes it as equivalent to wāw.
rows.anchor: وأو تقسيمية بمعنى الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second condition's mention of commanding piety fits the reading that forbidding a thing commands its opposite or entails that command; here the forbidding man urges idol worship. It is omitted from the first clause for brevity; action in prayer is a stronger practical call than speech.
rows.anchor: ولعل ذكر الأمر بالتقوى في الجملة الثانية لأن النهي على ما قيل كان عن الصلاة والأمر بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the prohibition occurred during prayer and thus could target both the prayer and its call to others: prayer perfects the worshipper, while preaching benefits others, so stopping him interrupted both.
rows.anchor: وقيل المذكور أولاً ليس النهي عن الصلاة بل النهي حين الصلاة وهو محتمل أن يكون لها أو لغيرها

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam reads the address throughout as directed to the Prophet: if the forbidding man had pursued guidance and urged piety, that would suit a rational, wealthy man better than disbelief and obstructing God's worship; the verse laments his lost higher station.
rows.anchor: وجوز الإمام كون الخطاب في الكل له عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: ʿIṣām al-Dīn reads 96:9 as evidence of the tyrant's arrogance when self-sufficient, 96:11 as reproach for losing the benefit of guidance and piety, 96:13 as reproach for earning punishment, and ألم يعلم as a severe threat.
rows.anchor: واعتبر عصام الدين هذه الجملة توبيخاً على تفويت ما ينفع وما بعدها توبيخاً على كسب ما يضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although revealed about Abū Jahl, the warning applies to everyone who stops prayer. It does not forbid objecting to prayer in usurped places or disliked times, since the objection concerns an accompanying attribute rather than prayer itself.
rows.anchor: ثم إن الآية وإن نزلت في أبي جهل عليه اللعنة لكن كل من نهى عن الصلاة ومنع منها فهو شريكه في الوعيد

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report says ʿAlī saw people praying before the ʿĪd prayer; when asked why he did not forbid them, he feared the warning in this verse. Another version says he preferred to tell them what he had seen the Prophet do rather than forbid a worshipper.
rows.anchor: فروي عن أمير المؤمنين كرم الله تعالى وجهه أنه رأى في المصلي أقواماً يصلون قبل صلاة العيد

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says Abū Ḥanīfa likewise avoided a direct prohibition: asked by Abū Yūsuf about a prayer formula while rising from bowing, he stated the formula he favored and continued to prostration without explicitly forbidding it.
rows.anchor: وقد سلك نحو هذا المسلك أبو حنيفة عليه الرحمة فقد روي أن أبا يوسف قال له أيقول المصلي حين يرفع رأسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning extends by analogy to forbidding other worship, whether by words or conduct; distracting someone from worship also counts as a practical prohibition, a widespread affliction.
rows.anchor: ويقاس على النهي عن الصلاة النهي عن غيرها من أنواع العبادة ولا فرق بين النهي القالي والنهي الحالي
